claims.text: The initial Q235 steel has homogeneous substrate properties.
A laser-metal-deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 HEA coating can suppress corrosion-related degradation of Q235 steel in harsh environments.
A continuous HEA coating suppresses corrosion by preventing electrolyte ingress to the Q235 substrate.
A continuous HEA coating minimizes galvanic coupling at the coating-substrate interface.
Laser deposition can generate thermal stresses and coating defects such as cracking.
Cracks and porosity provide pathways for corrosive agents to penetrate the coating.
Coating cracks or porosity can negate the coating's protective effect.
Exposed contact between a relatively noble HEA coating and carbon steel can galvanically accelerate corrosion of the steel.
Coating microstructural integrity at the coating-substrate interface controls barrier effectiveness and the propensity for local galvanic corrosion.
An optimized, continuous HEA coating will produce a significantly lower corrosion rate than untreated Q235 steel under identical exposure conditions.
An optimized, continuous HEA coating will reduce formation of iron-based corrosion products relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Deliberately defective coatings will cause more localized corrosion, thicker oxide layers, and greater weight loss than both defect-free coatings and uncoated Q235 steel.
Untreated Q235 steel will exhibit relatively high and uniform corrosion degradation because it lacks a protective coating.
Strong adhesion and coating continuity are boundary conditions for the proposed protection.
Extreme thermal cycling or a high defect density may eliminate the coating's protective benefit.
The corrosion-rate reduction depends on coating microstructure, environmental chemistry, and temperature.
A controlled study should compare uncoated, defect-minimized coated, and deliberately defected coated Q235 samples under otherwise identical room- and elevated-temperature exposures.

Failure of the optimized coating to significantly outperform the untreated reference, or failure of defective coatings to aggravate corrosion, would falsify the proposed combined barrier and defect-induced galvanic mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says a defective coating can produce more corrosion than the uncoated sample, whereas the baseline broadly characterizes untreated Q235 as having higher degradation because it lacks a barrier. The latter should be restricted to comparison with the intact coating.
